prime.problem: Without this step the manual backward pass stops at hprebn: you'd have gradients for W2, BatchNorm and tanh, but nothing for W1, b1 or the embedding table C, so the character vectors could never learn.
prime.fits: It is the last stretch of Exercise 1. It reuses the matmul-by-shapes rule from layer 2 and the idea that a value used many times collects the sum of its gradients, now applied to a table lookup.
expect: linear layer 1 backward (the same three lines as layer 2)
a lookup as many copies of one row
prime.goal: Write dembcat, dW1, db1, demb and dC from memory, explain why repeated characters need an add, and spot the one-liner that silently gets it wrong.

attend: Why does undoing view need no arithmetic at all, while undoing C[Xb] does?
The character '.' is looked up 29 times in this batch. Where do those 29 gradient rows end up, and how are they combined?
Why does dC[Xb] += demb run without error yet give the wrong answer, and which rows does it get wrong?
What happens to the rows of C for characters that no example in the batch used?
Why is db1 about 1e-9 even though the lab says it matches autograd exactly?

must: emb = C[Xb] copies one row of C per lookup → a character looked up m times is used m times → by the multi-use rule its gradient is the sum of m demb rows → dC[ix] += demb[k, j], a scatter-add
view only relabels the same 960 numbers in the same order → its local derivative is the identity → the backward is just dembcat.view(emb.shape), with no arithmetic

fancy-index dC[Xb] += demb reads, adds, then writes each index → for a repeated index the writes overwrite each other instead of adding → only repeated characters go wrong (12 rows here, maxdiff 0.0367), so the bug hides behind the correct single-use rows
hprebn = embcat @ W1 + b1 is a matmul plus a broadcast bias → same pattern as layer 2 → dhprebn @ W1.T, embcat.T @ dhprebn, dhprebn.sum(0), chosen by matching (32,30), (30,64), (64,)
elevated: BatchNorm subtracts the batch mean right after linear 1 → a constant added to every example (b1) cancels → db1 is about 2.3e-9, and b1 never learns anything useful
Rows of C that no example looked up get exactly 0 → those characters don't move this step → rare characters learn only on the batches that contain them
reference: the lab batch's counts: 96 lookups, 21 distinct characters, '.' ×29, 6 unused rows

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three forward lines that start the net and, next to each, its backward line(s) with shapes. Then explain in 2–3 sentences why the embedding backward is a sum and not a copy.
checklist: linear 1: dembcat = dhprebn @ W1.T, dW1 = embcat.T @ dhprebn, db1 = dhprebn.sum(0)
lookup: each of the 96 demb rows is added into row Xb[k, j] of dC
a forward copy (reuse) becomes a backward sum, so repeated characters must accumulate
unused characters get a zero row

retrieve.q: Explain, without code, what the gradient of the embedding table C means for one character, and why it depends on how often that character appears in the batch.
answer: row c of dC says how the loss changes if that character's vector moves
each lookup of c is one use, and uses add
more lookups → more rows summed; zero lookups → zero gradient

retrieve.q: Walk the double loop for example 25, whose context is . k o. Which rows of dC does it touch, with which rows of demb?
answer: dC[0] += demb[25, 0] for '.'
dC[11] += demb[25, 1] for 'k'
dC[15] += demb[25, 2] for 'o'
each adds to whatever other examples already put there

retrieve.q: You need the embedding backward inside a 200k-step training loop. Compare the Python double loop, index_add_ and the one-hot matmul: which do you pick, and what does each cost or risk?
answer: double loop: clearest, but 96 Python iterations every step
index_add_: one call, bit-exact, adds repeats correctly
one-hot matmul: also exact, but builds a 96 × 27 matrix and does 25,920 multiply-adds for 960 additions; grows with vocabulary
avoid dC[Xb] += demb: wrong for repeats

retrieve.q: Why is demb = dembcat.view(emb.shape) correct, and when would "just view back" be wrong?
answer: view keeps the same numbers in the same order, so gradient entry i maps back to the same entry i
it would be wrong if the forward reordered axes (permute or transpose); then you must reorder back

compare.q: dcounts needed += because counts fed two branches. dC needs += because rows are looked up many times. What is the same rule underneath, and how does the way each bug shows up in cmp differ?
answer: same rule: a value used more than once gets the sum of its uses' gradients
counts: every entry has two fixed paths, so forgetting one makes the whole tensor wrong
dC: the number of uses depends on the data, so only repeated rows go wrong and single-use rows still match

compare.q: Linear 1 and linear 2 have the same backward formulas. What changes between them, and why can shape matching still choose the arrangement uniquely?
answer: only the names and sizes: (32,30)@(30,64) vs (32,64)@(64,27)
32, 30 and 64 are all different, so only one arrangement fits each gradient
both biases get a sum over the batch, but db1 is about 0 because BatchNorm cancels it

compare.q: The forward lookup C[Xb] is the same as a one-hot vector times C. How does that view explain the backward, and why don't we compute it that way?
answer: one_hot @ C is a matmul, so its backward for C is one_hot.T @ demb, which is exactly the scatter-add
it's exact but wastes work on the zeros: 25,920 multiply-adds for 960 useful additions
indexing and scatter-add do only the useful part

predict.q: Delete the BatchNorm layer so hprebn goes straight into tanh. Would db1 still be about 1e-9? Commit, then reason about which forward step made it vanish.
predict.answer: No. The near-zero db1 comes from BatchNorm subtracting the batch mean, which cancels any constant added to every example. Without BatchNorm, b1 shifts each preactivation before tanh, so it changes the loss, and db1 = dhprebn.sum(0) becomes a real, non-zero gradient. The formula for db1 doesn't change; the incoming dhprebn does, since it no longer sums to zero across the batch.

apply.task: Break it and debug it. In labs/embedding-backward.py, replace the double loop with dC = torch.zeros_like(C); dC[Xb] += demb. Run it, then print which characters' rows differ from C.grad. Fix it with a one-liner that isn't index_add_.
apply.done: The broken version prints exact: False | approximate: False with maxdiff 0.0367, exactly 12 rows differ, and they are the 12 characters with a count above 1 in torch.bincount(Xb.view(-1)). Your fix prints exact: True.
apply.hint: index_put_((Xb.view(-1),), demb.view(-1, 10), accumulate=True) is exact; the key word is accumulate.
